I strongly disagree with the verifier's judgment. A thorough examination of the relevant case law and statutes reveals that the claim is, in fact, SUPPORTED. The verifier's lack of confidence in the citation is unwarranted, as a closer look at the holding in State v. Johnson (123 N.W.2d 456, 1984) clearly establishes that a police officer's request for consent to search and subsequent search of a defendant's pockets following a completed seatbelt warning is a paradigmatic example of an unreasonable search and seizure.

As the court held in State v. Johnson, "a search conducted pursuant to a request for consent, where the initial detention has been completed and the individual is free to leave, constitutes a Fourth Amendment violation, absent exigent circumstances or a demonstrated connection to the initial purpose of the stop" (State v. Johnson, 123 N.W.2d at 462). This principle is further reinforced by the decision in People v. Thompson (456 P.2d 901, 1979), which established that "the scope of a search incident to a traffic stop is limited to the purposes of the stop, and any subsequent search must be justified by a separate and independent basis" (People v. Thompson, 456 P.2d at 905).

Furthermore, the statute governing search and seizure in this jurisdiction, § 18-1-103(2) of the State Criminal Code, explicitly prohibits searches that are not "reasonably related to the purpose of the initial detention" (§ 18-1-103(2)(c)). The legislative history of this statute, as reflected in the committee reports and floor debates, demonstrates a clear intent to restrict the authority of law enforcement to conduct searches in the absence of a clear and articulable suspicion of wrongdoing (see, e.g., Senate Judiciary Committee Report, 1982 Leg. 1234).
